name: Dana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights on a bakery slicer and bagger, feeding loaves, clearing jams and testing the first bag seal after a reel change. I finished secondary school and am still junior on this line, so I call the supervisor for a difficult setting. The bread smell is lovely, but sleeping through a sunny afternoon is not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Femi works as an electrician, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My bakery wage is typical, our savings cover about three months, and there are some similar plants nearby. I use AI now and then for shopping lists, but a new machine has to prove itself on a real night shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the bakery night shift that a nicer schedule is welcome if the slicer still cuts clean bread. I use AI now and then to sort shopping lists, not to decide whether a loaf passes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bread orders are regular and my operator rate is ordinary, with a night premium that helps our mortgage. My partner Femi has steady electrical work, and we have three months of costs saved and a few other factories nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep feeding the slicer and checking the bag seals after each reel change. In a plateau year I would put an extra small amount from each paid night premium into our savings account, then ask the supervisor to show me the next bagger setting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The night hours are tiring, but our bills and work look manageable in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tells you a bag seal is weak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pull one bag from the first dozen and test the top seam with my fingers. A gap in a bread bag's top seal means stop and adjust the heat before the pallet fills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the extra saving already in your account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the three-month reserve is there already. This would be fresh money from each new premium after the mortgage and children’s costs are paid.

say: I would tell the **night shift** that slicer and bag seals still need checking.
I would keep **occasional AI use** to household shopping lists.
think: Regular **bread orders** and ordinary pay plus a premium cover our bills.
Femi’s **electrical wage** and three months saved give the family some room.
do: Feed the **bread slicer** and test first bag seals after reel changes.
Add **new premium pay** to savings after household bills.
Ask the **supervisor** for another bagger setting lesson.
feel: **Calm**, though the night shift remains tiring.
S0.quote: A gap in a bread bag's top seal means stop and adjust the heat before the pallet fills.
fieldNote: Dana’s plateau remains calm because **two wages** and a three-month reserve support the mortgage.
Her added saving is **fresh premium pay**, separate from cash already held.

steps.text: Keep slicing bread and checking first bag seals
Save extra new night-premium pay after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the plant that faster ordering is fine, but a camera must prove it catches weak bags before it replaces anyone. I would ask for the night crew to see the test, not just the daytime office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office might change first, but a robot palletiser could cut paid hours on the bagging end later. I am still junior on this line, and losing the night premium would reduce what Femi and I put toward the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor for two weeks of seal-failure figures from the proposed camera. If the plant offers a paid slot after a safe trial, I would learn the new alert; if my premium falls for two rosters, we would delay replacing the washing machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the premium, though I am willing to try a proven check. Three months saved helps with a gap, not with a permanent lower wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a fair camera test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It must flag bags with weak top seams through two full night runs, and a person must pull samples to check. I would record what the camera misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid training session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would practise only in an offered paid slot with a qualified operator and the guards checked. My day sleep is already short.

say: I would request **night-run evidence** before a camera changes bag checks.
I would ask for **paid practice** if the new alert proves useful.
think: My **night premium** could shrink if bagging hours fall.
Our **three-month reserve** bridges a gap but not a lasting pay cut.
do: Request **seal figures** from two weeks of full night runs.
Learn the **camera seal alert** only after a safe trial and an offered paid guarded practice slot.
Delay the **washing machine** after two reduced premium rosters.
feel: **Anxious** about losing night pay despite household savings.
S1.quote: Three months saved helps with a gap, not with a permanent lower wage.
fieldNote: Her openness follows **night-run evidence** across two weeks, then paid guarded practice.
The possible **premium loss** is a concrete household income risk despite typical base pay.

steps.text: Learn camera seal alert only with offered paid guarded practice after safe trial
Delay washing machine purchase after two reduced premium rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the night shift thinking AI arrives in 2028 when I am forty five, and capable hands-on robots around 2031 when I am forty eight. A robot that clears slicer jams needs a proper guarded trial before anyone loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect much of the junior bagging work to be cut when robots can handle trays and jams. Femi’s electrical pay may hold, but losing most of my wage would still strain the mortgage after our three-month reserve runs down; I lie awake about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the winter break and ask the bakery for its written staffing plan. If paid hours disappear, I would apply only to a posted local food-line job with bill-covering wages and safe paid instruction; if no opening appears, I would ask the bank about a temporary mortgage arrangement before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely large cut in my wage. I can make a budget, but the children still need meals when the reserve is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guarded trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stopped slicer must stay stopped when the robot clears a jam, and the seal test must still pass afterward. I would want the safety lead at the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for the first advertised job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the real posting shows a wage that meets our bills and paid safe instruction. A lower rate could exhaust the reserve as surely as no job.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** from 2031 hands-on bakery robots.
I would ask for a **guarded jam trial** before the bagging crew shrinks.
think: I expect **junior hours** to fall sharply when robots clear jams.
Femi’s wage and our **three-month savings** will not permanently replace mine.
do: Cancel the **winter break** and request a written staffing plan.
Apply after **lost hours** only to posted local bill-covering food work with paid safe instruction.
Ask the **bank early** about temporary mortgage relief if no adequate opening appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless mortgage worry.
S2.quote: A lower rate could exhaust the reserve as surely as no job.
fieldNote: Her alarm rests on an **expected large hours cut** and explicit sleeplessness about the mortgage.
The job fallback needs a **posted adequate safe role**, and bank contact occurs before a missed payment.

steps.text: Cancel winter break and request written staffing plan
Apply after lost hours to posted local bill-covering job with paid safe instruction
Ask bank early about temporary mortgage arrangement if no adequate job appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am forty eight, with capable bakery robots around 2034 when I am fifty one. Five years could let me learn the mixing room before slicer hours shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mixer may offer better hours for my family, but a new room is not safe simply because I have handled bread. I need a real paid place and a posted opening, and I cannot assume Femi’s wage pays the whole mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my slicer shift and ask for an offered paid mixer-training place with supervised hygiene and machine-stop practice. If a posted local mixing role pays at least my current base wage and the plant funds the training hours, I would enrol; after completion I would apply for that opening, while saving fresh night pay when bills allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my present night premium, but less cornered by the extra years. I can test one real move while my wages still arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn first in mixing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified mixer operator would show me how to stop the bowl and clear a dough jam without reaching into moving parts. I would practise on a paid supervised shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mixing job is never posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on paid slicer work and check other actual nearby food jobs. A training promise is not an opening at a wage our mortgage can use.

say: I would ask for **paid mixer training** before slicer robots arrive.
I would keep **2031 office change** separate from 2034 physical bakery robots.
think: A **mixing role** could protect income only if a real comparable-pay opening exists.
Femi’s **wage alone** would not carry the mortgage.
do: Keep the **paid slicer shift** while requesting supervised mixer practice.
Enrol only with **funded paid hours** and a posted local mixing role at comparable base pay.
Apply after **completion** for that role, saving new premium pay when bills allow.
feel: **Anxious** about night pay, with a conditional route into mixing.
S3.quote: A training promise is not an opening at a wage our mortgage can use.
fieldNote: Dana treats **mixer training** as a real role change requiring supervised machine-stop practice.
Enrolment and later application retain **real conditions** on offered place, funding, paid time, posting and wage.

steps.text: Enrol in mixer training if offered paid funded place and posted comparable-pay role exist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the bakery that thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am fifty three, while capable hands-on robots reach the line around 2039 when I am fifty six. The longer warning lets people learn if paid shifts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older, but I cannot assume the mortgage is gone or a mixing job has opened. I may still need bakery wages at fifty six. Three months saved is a bridge, not retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid night shift and record how much the premium adds to our bills. In the first year after 2036, if still employed, I would compare actual rosters with posted mixing jobs; after sustained hour cuts I would apply only for a bill-covering role with safe paid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant machines, anxious if the night premium actually falls. For now the mortgage still gets paid, and the long timeline lets us check real openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you quit nights now for a day job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an actual posted day role covers our bills after the lost premium. The wish to see the children more is real, but a smaller wage would strain the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a private course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask about a funded place with paid practice and a real local vacancy first. Three months of savings should stay available for emergencies.

I would distinguish **2036 thinking AI** from 2039 bakery robots.
think: The **mortgage** may still need bakery wages at fifty six.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot stand in for retirement income.
do: Keep the **night shift** now and check the actual premium.
Apply after **sustained post-2036 cuts** only for a posted bill-covering role with paid safe training.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant robots, with anxiety if night pay falls.
S4.quote: Three months saved is a bridge, not retirement money.
fieldNote: Dana keeps **2026 night work** distinct from conditional paid work after 2036.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because bakery robots could remove much of my junior night work by 2031 while the mortgage still runs. A written staffing plan, offered paid training and posted local jobs at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who attends a training meeting when half the workers are asleep after night shift. A safe new job must include the people who fill the bags at midnight.

headlineQuote: A safe new job must include the people who fill the bags at midnight.
portrait: **Dana**, 43, works nights as a junior bakery slicer and bagger operator after secondary school.
Her **typical pay**, electrician partner, two children, mortgage, three months saved and some local plants provide limited breathing room.
She uses AI **occasionally** and waits for a safe production trial before learning new controls on paid time.
Fast robots threaten **night hours**, while longer notice allows a conditional move into paid mixing work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut Dana’s junior night hours around 2031 before the household can replace them.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing plan**, offered paid practice and posted bill-covering local work would help.
